\section*{Limitations}
\label{sec:limitations}

All eight generators are base (pretrained) models.
This is a deliberate design choice: base models isolate the generation mechanism from instruction-tuning effects and enable controlled study of recursive distributional drift.
However, web text is predominantly produced by instruction-tuned and RLHF-aligned models.
Preliminary instruct experiments confirm that depth signal degrades substantially under instruction tuning: OLMo-2-1B-Instruct drops to LOGO F1\,=\,0.338 (vs.\ 0.763 base) and Qwen3-0.6B with chat template to 0.667 (vs.\ 0.816 base); these comparisons use earlier LOGO subsets (5--6 generators) predating the full 8-generator expansion in Table~\ref{tab:logo-results}.
Length-matched analysis yields near-zero correlations ($|\rho| < 0.02$) and binary classification near chance (F1\,$\approx$\,0.5) for Qwen models, leaving interpretation ambiguous.
Extending depth profiling to instruct models requires addressing these confounds (length regulation, format constraints, safety-driven distribution shaping) that instruction tuning introduces.

Our experiments include generators up to 8.2B parameters (Qwen3-8B).
Depth signal persists at this scale (Qwen3-8B 3-class F1\,=\,0.714), but cross-scale transfer incurs a moderate gap vs.\ $\leq$2.8B generators (F1\,=\,0.77--0.81).
Frontier models (70B+) and closed-source models remain untested; the consistent scale trend (Mistral-7B binary F1\,=\,0.633, lowest among all generators) suggests depth signal may weaken further at frontier scales, potentially approaching the detection floor.

Differential depth response strength is prompt-type dependent: continuation chains show strongest drift (within-type binary F1\,=\,0.781) compared to elaboration (0.730) and rewriting (0.737), with within-prompt-type paraphrastic chains showing weaker signal (binary F1\,=\,0.671 vs.\ 0.749 for within-prompt-type continuation).
DDR is most reliably detected in continuation-style generation; near-paraphrastic settings approach the method's detection floor.
Cross-prompt-type transfer (LOPTO F1\,=\,0.753) confirms shared signal, yet additional prompt types (e.g., summarization, instruction following) and cross-generator $\times$ cross-prompt interactions remain untested.

Our primary evaluation uses single-generator chains; cross-model chains (\S\ref{sec:results-classification}) confirm depth signal under generator heterogeneity (3-class F1\,=\,0.809, binary F1\,=\,0.764), though the eight generators represent a controlled laboratory setting rather than the full diversity of real-world contamination.
Simulated human editing (\S\ref{sec:discussion}) suggests graceful degradation, but the gap between simulated token replacement and real-world post-processing remains untested.

The reference model is fixed to Pythia-410M throughout, although cross-family reference experiments (\S\ref{sec:results-differential}) confirm the phenomenon is not reference-specific (spread 0.013 across three references).
All seed texts in the main evaluation are English Wikipedia excerpts.
Cross-domain evaluation (Appendix~\ref{app:domain}) at both $t{=}1.0$ and $t{=}0.7$ shows that depth signal persists across News, Academic, and Code domains (binary F1 0.63--0.75 depending on domain and temperature), though a domain $\times$ temperature interaction exists: at $t{=}0.7$, Academic domain binary F1 drops to 0.628, suggesting that reference model calibration is critical for cross-domain deployment.
The reference model dependency (Pythia-410M, English-centric pretraining) limits non-English applicability and adds inference overhead relative to surface-feature-only approaches.
Generalization to other languages remains untested.

Our default analysis uses fixed decoding parameters (temperature 0.7, nucleus $p{=}0.9$). A temperature ablation across four generators from three families (Appendix~\ref{app:sampling-sensitivity}) shows that the method operates reliably within $t \in [0.5, 0.7]$ but degrades at $t{=}0.9$ ($-9.3$ to $-26.0$\,pp across generators). Low-temperature improvement is model-dependent (Pythia/OLMo: $+7$--$9$\,pp; Qwen: $0$--$2$\,pp), indicating that depth profiling assumes standard decoding regimes and that the benefit of conservative temperature varies by model family.
Tokenizer differences across families may contribute to the observed temperature sensitivity pattern; within-family comparisons (two Qwen models showing consistent robustness) support a family-level effect, but controlling for tokenizer requires further study.

Our baselines repurpose detection scores as depth predictors but do not include simple n-gram frequency profiles, which could serve as an additional surface-level baseline for the depth classification task.

We use 3-class granularity (gen-0\,/\,gen-1\,/\,gen-2+). A 5-class evaluation (Appendix~\ref{app:finer-depth}) yields LOGO F1\,$\approx$\,0.50, with depths 2--4 mutually indistinguishable, validating the 3-class design as the practical resolution limit.

[审稿报告]
Overall: 3.0 (Findings)

# Round 24 审稿报告 — gen-depth-fingerprint

**论文**: Depth Profiling: Classifying Recursive Generation Depth in Base LLM Text Chains
**Venue**: EMNLP 2026 via ACL Rolling Review (Long Paper)
**Reviewer 编排**: 2 人（R1: 方法严谨性+实验设计+统计推断；R2: 新颖性+完整性+写作质量+格式合规）
**轮次**: Round 1 + 交叉分享（1 轮收敛）
**外部审稿**: 未配置

---

## Summary

本文提出 generation depth classification 任务——将文本分类为 gen-0（人类）/ gen-1（首次生成）/ gen-2+（递归生成），取代传统二分类检测。通过 7 个手工特征（5 个参考模型 NLL 统计量 + 2 个表面词汇多样性特征）和 XGBoost 分类器，在 8 个 base model generator（Pythia/OLMo/Qwen/Llama/Mistral，0.6B–8B）上实现 LOGO binary F1=0.694。核心发现是 differential depth response (DDR)：特征分为 drifting（entropy mean, TTR, hapax ratio）、intermediate（entropy std）和 near-stationary（entropy max, tail decay, entropy min）三组，与递归生成下 NLL location shift / shape stability 的解释一致。论文诚实地将贡献定位为 "empirical rather than methodological"。

---

## Strengths

**S1. 新颖且有实际意义的任务定义。** [R1,R2 共识] 从 binary real-vs-synthetic 推进到 ordinal depth classification 是有意义的方向扩展，与 model collapse 和数据溯源有清晰关联。这是一个之前未被正式定义的研究问题。

**S2. 评估协议严谨且透明。** [R1,R2 共识] LOGO + LOFO 双重评估，配套 independent-seed、length matching、cross-domain、cross-temperature、prompt type sensitivity 等多项控制实验。覆盖度在 EMNLP 投稿中属上乘。

**S3. 诚实的学术态度。** [R1,R2 共识] 论文主动标注 gen-0 seed sharing 问题、下游 n=3 局限、QLoRA 天花板与手工特征的 tradeoff。Limitations section 详尽（34 行，8+ 项局限）。

**S4. 可解释的方法设计。** [R1,R2 共识] 7 个手工特征完全透明可分析，DDR 框架为理解递归生成下文本属性的演化提供了有用的概念结构。

**S5. 附录覆盖全面。** [R1,R2 共识] 20+ 页附录涵盖 16 个实验板块，覆盖了几乎所有可预见的审稿问题。

**S6. 与 concurrent work 定位清晰。** [R2] 对 Broken Telephone 和 Markovian Chains 的区分有说服力，三个独立工作收敛于 ~3 class ceiling 的讨论增强了可信度。

---

## Weaknesses

### Critical

**N1. Base model 限制严重削弱论文 significance。** [R2 Critical, R1 Major]
- OLMo-2-1B-Instruct LOGO F1 从 0.763 暴跌至 0.338；Llama 3-class F1 从 0.742 降至 0.544
- 现实 web text 几乎全部由 instruct/RLHF 模型生成，base model 直接生成的文本在实际场景中极为罕见
- 论文将此框架为设计选择（"We restrict to base models, since instruction-tuning introduces confounds"），但实质是核心限制
- R1 认为对于 foundational study 此范围界定合理，R2 认为这严重削弱 impact
- **Director 判定**: Major-Critical。论文标题已含 "Base LLM"，scope 透明；但缺少 concrete deployment scenario 论证 base-model study 的独立实际价值

**N2. DDR tri-partition 阈值缺乏 principled 依据。** [R1 Critical, R2 同意降为 Major]
- Cohen's d 阈值 0.75 介于惯例 medium (0.5) 和 large (0.8) 之间，未说明选择理由
- 敏感性分析仅覆盖 near-stationary boundary，未检验 drifting boundary
- 若阈值降至 0.5，entropy_std (d=0.55) 将从 intermediate 重分类为 drifting，改变 DDR 叙事
- R2 指出 data-driven clustering (silhouette=0.632) 和 9.5× gap 提供了独立验证
- **Director 判定**: Major。data-driven 验证降低了风险，但阈值选择仍需 justification

**N3. 下游效用实验 n=3 seeds 严重 underpowered。** [R1 Critical, R2 初标 Minor 后同意升级]
- n=3 时 TOST power 极低，论文自承 Cohen's d "unreliable"
- Discussion §5 L17 仍做定性结论（"depth composition does not determine training utility"），该声明无法由 n=3 支撑
- 虽已从 contribution list 移除，但 Discussion 中的结论措辞需降格为 "preliminary evidence"

### Major

**W1. 三个 drifting 特征本质是同一 latent factor。** [R1,R2 强烈共识]
- entropy mean、TTR、hapax ratio 相关性 r=0.81-0.97，PCA 92.3% by PC1
- DDR 3/1/3 在独立信息维度上更接近 1/1/3
- 论文自承 permutation importance 差异反映 feature masking 而非独立信号
- "7-feature ensemble" / "three drifting features" 的表述可能误导读者关于独立信息维度数量

**W2. DDR 作为 EMNLP 核心贡献偏薄。** [R1,R2 共识]
- 核心发现是 "some features are more sensitive to recursive generation than others" 的系统化表述
- 自承 "post-hoc and empirical"，无理论解释，缺乏 predictive power
- 作为 Findings 贡献合适，不够 main conference
- 需要更严谨的 mechanistic explanation 或形式化分析来增强深度

**W3. Contribution #3 (parameter dependence) 本质是 negative result。** [R1,R2 共识]
- 将 "方法在某些条件下失效"（instruction tuning, t=0.9）列为贡献逻辑不自洽
- R1 指出温度 boundary condition 有操作价值
- 建议 reframe 为 Discussion 中的 "boundary conditions"

**W4. Independent-seed 控制覆盖率不足。** [R1,R2 共识]
- 仅 2/8 generators (Pythia-2.8B, OLMo-2-1B)，覆盖 2/5 家族
- F1 差距可忽略 (0.680 vs 0.694)，但 Qwen/Llama/Mistral 未验证

### Minor

**M1. LOGO 同家族泄漏未在 Table 1 体现。** [R1 Major, R2 降级] LOFO 0.686 vs LOGO 0.694，差 0.8pp。建议 Table 1 增加 LOFO 行。

**M2. Abstract 数字过多。** [R1,R2 共识] 7+ 个具体数值，建议精简至 2-3 个。

**M3. Related Work 缺少 ordinal classification in NLP 讨论。** [R1,R2 共识] 论文将 task 框架为 ordinal classification 但 Related Work 无对应子章节。

**M4. Pooled Cohen's d 异方差问题仅在附录讨论。** [R1,R2 共识] 正文需添加 caveat。

**M5. 未探索 n-gram/句法特征，缺少相关引用。** [R1,R2 共识]

---

## Reviewer Consensus [AGREE]

1. **Overall 3.0 (Findings)**: 两位 Reviewer 独立给出相同评分
2. **任务定义新颖 + 实验严谨 → 达到 Findings 门槛**
3. **DDR 贡献偏 empirical + base-model 限制 + 性能偏低 → 不够 Conference**
4. **Contribution #3 定位不当**: 需 reframe
5. **三个 drifting 特征高度冗余**: 3/1/3 叙事需调整
6. **下游 n=3 underpowered**: 结论措辞需降格
7. **附录覆盖和学术诚实度为论文最突出优点**

## Reviewer Divergence [REBUT]

1. **Base model 限制严重程度**: R2=Critical（实际场景失效）vs R1=Major（foundational study 合理范围）。Director 判定 Major-Critical：scope 透明但需补充 deployment scenario 论证。

2. **F1=0.694 是否偏低**: R2=Major（QLoRA 0.905 说明远非最优）vs R1=REBUT（指标不可比：8-gen binary LOGO vs 6-gen 3-class QLoRA；LOGO 是极严格评估；QLoRA 高 F1 恰恰支持 depth signal 存在）。Director 判定：R1 论据更有力——R2 的对比存在指标和评估集不匹配问题。F1=0.694 在 LOGO 下对 foundational study 可接受。

3. **R1-W2 参考模型 confound**: R1 声称 cross-reference F1 降至 ~0.613。R2 核查发现 R1 数据引用错误（0.613 来自 Appendix H perturbation experiment，非 cross-reference；实际 spread=0.013）。**R1 未在交叉回应中反驳此点。Director 判定：R1-W2 dismissed**，参考模型 confound 不构成实质问题。

4. **下游 n=3 严重程度**: R1=Critical vs R2=Minor。R1 在交叉回应中成功说服 R2 升级。Director 判定：论文已将 downstream 从 contribution list 移除，降为 Major-Critical——需修改 Discussion 措辞但不再影响核心评分。

---

## Questions for Authors

**Q1.** [R2, R1 同意] 请具体描述 base-model depth profiling 的实际部署场景。在什么现实应用中需要判断文本经历了多少代 base model 递归生成？

**Q2.** [R1] 若将 drifting 阈值从 0.75 降至 0.5，DDR 的三分叙事如何变化？请提供 drifting boundary 的完整敏感性分析。

**Q3.** [R2] QLoRA 端到端模型在 instruct model 上的表现如何？它是否能部分克服 base model 限制？

**Q4.** [R1] 三个 drifting 特征替换为其第一主成分后，分类性能是否变化？这能直接检验它们是否携带独立信息。

**Q5.** [R2] Cross-model chains F1=0.764 高于 LOGO 0.694——depth signal 在 generator 混合时反而更强？R1 指出评估协议差异（5-fold CV vs LOGO）可能解释部分 gap。

---

## Missing References

- **Ordinal classification in NLP**: 缺少 ordinal classification 在 NLP 任务中的应用文献（如 sentiment ordinal approaches） [R1,R2 共识]
- **N-gram based detection methods**: 论文特征集不含 n-gram 特征，需引用相关方法 contextualize 特征选择 [R1,R2 共识]
- **Distribution shift 文献**: DDR 本质是 distribution shift 现象，可引用经典框架（covariate shift, dataset shift）[R2, R1 部分同意]

---

## Overall Assessment

**Overall: 3.0 (Findings)**

|------|----|----|------|
| Soundness | 3/5 | 4/5 | 3.5/5 |
| Excitement | 3.5/5 | 2.5/5 | 3/5 |
| Reproducibility | 4/5 | 4/5 | 4/5 |

\section{Discussion}
\label{sec:discussion}

The DDR tri-partition (3 drifting / 1 intermediate / 3 near-stationary) is consistent with a location/shape decomposition: under fixed temperature $\tau$ and nucleus $p$, the softmax output distribution's shape (variance, tail behavior) is constrained by the decoding configuration, while iterative conditioning shifts the input distribution's location as text becomes increasingly predictable to the reference model.
This interpretation is post-hoc and empirical; formal analysis of softmax output distribution dynamics under recursive conditioning remains an open problem.
DDR is an empirical decomposition capturing this dichotomy, not a claimed universal law of recursive generation.
DDR as characterized here is a parameter-dependent phenomenon (modulated by temperature and prompt type), not an intrinsic property of recursive generation independent of decoding conditions.
Temperature and prompt-type ablations (\S\ref{sec:results-differential}) support this as a tendency rather than a guarantee: all four tested generators degrade at $t{=}0.9$ ($-9.3$ to $-26.0$\,pp), and the signal varies across prompt types.

Instruction tuning substantially weakens the signal across all three tested families (OLMo, Qwen, Llama; Appendix~\ref{app:instruct}).
Within-model 3-class F1 drops 3.7--19.9\,pp (OLMo: 0.575 vs.\ 0.754; Qwen: 0.732 vs.\ 0.769; Llama: 0.544 vs.\ 0.742), while binary F1 changes remain small ($\Delta \leq 3.2$\,pp), indicating that instruction tuning primarily disrupts the gen-0/gen-1 boundary.
Under cross-generator evaluation, the degradation is larger (OLMo-Instruct LOGO F1\,=\,0.338 vs.\ 0.763 base).
Entropy-mean $\rho$ reverses sign consistently ($+0.48$ for OLMo and Qwen, $+0.23$ for Llama; all base models ${\approx}{-}0.6$), and 6 of 7 features reverse direction for OLMo and Qwen, 3 of 7 for Llama, consistent with instruction tuning shifting the generation attractor rather than destroying the iterative dynamics.
This restricts current applicability to base models; at the document level, within-model gen-1 per-class F1\,=\,0.63 (average across three instruct families; Appendix~\ref{app:instruct}) suffices for corpus-level flagging but not automated filtering (Appendix~\ref{app:error-analysis}).
Cross-temperature transfer degrades substantially at $t{=}1.0$ (Appendix~\ref{app:cross-temp}).
DDR characterizes distributional structure under recursive generation; depth profiling identifies this structure rather than prescribing data-selection actions.
A preliminary downstream experiment ($n{=}3$ seeds; Appendix~\ref{app:downstream}) found that depth composition does not determine training utility at fixed sample count, consistent with this diagnostic role, though the specific downstream finding requires validation at larger scale.

The QLoRA end-to-end classifier (3-class F1\,=\,0.905; Appendix~\ref{app:qlora}) confirms that richer representations capture depth signal well beyond the 7-feature set; at binary F1\,=\,0.694, the handcrafted ensemble trades classification ceiling for interpretability, enabling the DDR decomposition that end-to-end classifiers cannot provide.

% Abstract — Depth Profiling of Recursive LLM Generation Chains
\begin{abstract}
Text generated by large language models (LLMs) increasingly re-enters the web and seeds subsequent generation, producing recursive chains that progressively diverge from human-written text.
We study this phenomenon in base (pretrained) models and ask whether the drift is structured enough to classify how many generation steps a text has undergone, framing this as \emph{generation depth classification} (gen-0\,/\,gen-1\,/\,gen-2+ rather than binary real-vs-synthetic).
Across eight base models from five families (0.6B--8B parameters), we identify a \emph{differential depth response} (DDR): features partition into drifting (Cohen's $d > 0.75$), intermediate, and near-stationary ($d < 0.10$) groups under standard decoding ($t \leq 0.7$), consistent with recursive generation shifting the NLL location while distributional shape remains stable.
A 7-feature ensemble achieves leak-free binary F1\,=\,0.694 (95\% CI [.688, .700]) under leave-one-generator-out evaluation, generalizing across model families.
The depth signal degrades substantially under instruction tuning, restricting current applicability to base models.
\end{abstract}

\section{Related Work}
\label{sec:related}

\subsection{AI-Generated Text Detection}
\label{sec:related-detection}

Methods for distinguishing human-written from machine-generated text have evolved from statistical tests \cite{gltr,grover,release_strategies} to zero-shot reference-model approaches \cite{detectgpt,fast_detectgpt,binoculars,dna_gpt} and learned classifiers that combine handcrafted features with neural architectures \cite{ghostbuster,feat_aug_transformer,abburi_multifaceted,reliable_detection,ld_score}.
Recent work pursues diverse signals including intrinsic dimensionality \cite{intrinsic_dimension}, surprisal diversity \cite{diveye}, and distributional gap measures \cite{generator_barrier}; see \citet{tang2024science}, \citet{wu_survey_2025}, and \citet{jawahar_survey} for surveys.
A persistent limitation is that these methods produce binary (real vs.\ synthetic) decisions.
Recent work moves beyond binary detection along several axes.
\citet{beyond_binary} classify text into four roles (human-only, LLM-polished, LLM-expanded, LLM-only) via involvement measurement, discriminating production \emph{modes} rather than recursive depth.
\citet{two_birds} jointly detect machine-generated text and attribute it to specific LLMs, and \citet{beyond_final_actor} distinguish dual creator-editor roles across four production modes.
Multi-generator attribution, including generator-level classification in SemEval 2024 Task 8 Subtask B \cite{semeval2024_task8} and the DeFactify dataset \cite{defactify_dataset}, discriminates among different \emph{sources}.
All these approaches classify text by its production process or authorship, while our depth classification tracks how many recursive generation steps a text has undergone, an orthogonal axis.
Even when detection scores correlate with depth, they exhibit high cross-generator variance as ordinal predictors (binary F1 from 0.52 to 0.71; Table~\ref{tab:baselines}), because each captures a single distributional property that generalizes inconsistently \cite{paraphrase_evades,detection_possibilities}.
Our contribution is not a new detection method but the task formulation (generation depth classification, framed within the broader ordinal classification literature \cite{gutierrez_ordinal_survey,coral_ordinal,corn_ordinal}) and the finding that combining drifting, intermediate, and near-stationary features yields consistent cross-generator performance.
This is orthogonal to source attribution \cite{uchendu_attribution,munir_looking_glass}, which identifies \emph{which} model generated text; our LOGO evaluation decouples generator identity from depth.

\subsection{Model Collapse and Iterative Generation}
\label{sec:related-collapse}

Iterative generation can degrade text quality through two distinct mechanisms: \emph{training-loop} drift, where models retrained on their own outputs progressively lose distributional coverage, and \emph{inference-chain} drift, where a fixed model generates text conditioned on its own prior output without retraining.
Self-consuming generative models progressively lose distributional coverage \cite{self_consuming_mad}, and model collapse is inevitable without fresh human data \cite{curse_of_recursion}, though careful data mixing can mitigate this \cite{model_collapse_avoidable,strong_model_collapse}.
Self-training and self-play approaches \cite{self_rewarding_lms,spin} also involve iterative self-generation but optimize a training objective; these studies focus on training-loop degradation, whereas our setting studies inference chains.
The distinction extends beyond setting: model collapse erodes distributional tail coverage irreversibly as training progresses \cite{curse_of_recursion,strong_model_collapse}. In contrast, the inference-chain drift we observe is fully reversible under fixed parameters, and distributional shape exhibits negligible depth effects (Cohen's $d < 0.10$; \S\ref{sec:results-differential}).
The drifting/intermediate/near-stationary tri-partition central to our analysis has no analogue in model collapse studies, which track aggregate divergence without separating location from shape components.
Two concurrent works are most directly relevant.
\citet{broken_telephone} analyze paraphrasing and translation chains, showing progressive information loss under semantic-preservation constraints that confine depth signal to surface-level lexical decay.
\citet{markovian_chains} demonstrate that such constraints induce Markovian attractor dynamics bounding distinguishable depth to approximately three classes.
Both study paraphrastic chains; we differ in three respects: (i) non-paraphrastic continuation chains permit richer drift (both semantic and distributional); (ii) handcrafted features enable the DDR decomposition into drifting, intermediate, and near-stationary components; and (iii) our tri-partition reveals \emph{what} converges (location) versus what remains stable (shape), while their analyses characterize \emph{that} convergence occurs.
That all three works independently converge on approximately three distinguishable classes reflects different mechanisms reaching the same ceiling: Markovian attractor dynamics in semantic space \cite{markovian_chains}, surface-level lexical decay under paraphrastic constraints \cite{broken_telephone}, and feature-space compression in continuation chains (inter-class KS drops from 0.28 to 0.09 after depth 2; this work).

\subsection{Vocabulary Diversity and Stylometry}
\label{sec:related-diversity}

Declining lexical diversity in LLM-generated text is documented in both training \cite{curious_decline} and deployment \cite{writing_diversity} settings.
Our surface features (TTR and hapax ratio) are classical stylometric measures \cite{stamatatos_survey,koppel_authorship,neal2017surveying}; more sophisticated alternatives exist (MTLD, HD-D \cite{mccarthy2010mtld}; MATTR \cite{covington2010mattr}) but TTR and hapax ratio suffice for depth discrimination.
We push beyond generator identity \cite{uchendu_attribution} to the \emph{depth} dimension under top-$p$ sampling \cite{nucleus_sampling}.

\subsection{Data Quality and Provenance}
\label{sec:related-provenance}

Scalable data curation relies on quality signals \cite{dsir,qurating,ccnet}, and recent work highlights the challenge of detecting training data contamination \cite{oren2024proving,golchin2024time} and maintaining data provenance at scale \cite{longpre2024data}.
Generation depth is a complementary provenance signal characterizing \emph{how many steps removed} text is from a human source.
Proactive watermarking \cite{watermark_llm,synthid_text,aaronson_watermark} embeds identifiable patterns, but watermark strength decays across multi-step chains \cite{chainwash}, which motivates passive post-hoc methods like ours.
At the feature level, our NLL analysis connects to \citet{min_k_percent}, who use the probability tail for membership inference; we analyze the full NLL distribution for generation depth classification.

% Abstract — Depth Profiling of Recursive LLM Generation Chains
\begin{abstract}
Text generated by large language models (LLMs) increasingly re-enters the web and seeds subsequent generation, producing recursive chains that progressively diverge from human-written text.
We study this phenomenon in base (pretrained) models and ask whether the drift is structured enough to classify how many generation steps a text has undergone, framing this as \emph{generation depth classification} (gen-0\,/\,gen-1\,/\,gen-2+ rather than binary real-vs-synthetic).
Across eight base models from five families (0.6B--8B parameters), we identify a \emph{differential depth response} (DDR): features partition into drifting ($d > 0.75$), intermediate, and near-stationary ($d < 0.10$) groups, consistent with recursive generation shifting the NLL location while distributional shape remains stable.
A 7-feature ensemble achieves leak-free binary F1\,=\,0.694 under leave-one-generator-out evaluation, generalizing across model families.
The depth signal degrades substantially under instruction tuning, restricting current applicability to base models.
\end{abstract}

% Abstract — Depth Profiling of Recursive LLM Generation Chains
\begin{abstract}
Text generated by large language models (LLMs) increasingly re-enters the web and seeds subsequent generation, producing recursive chains that progressively diverge from human-written text.
We study this phenomenon in base (pretrained) models and ask whether the drift is structured enough to classify how many generation steps a text has undergone, framing this as \emph{generation depth classification} (gen-0\,/\,gen-1\,/\,gen-2+ rather than binary real-vs-synthetic).
Across eight base models from five families (0.6B--8B parameters), we identify a \emph{differential depth response} (DDR): features partition into drifting ($d{=}0.76$--$1.17$), intermediate, and near-stationary ($d < 0.10$) groups, consistent with recursive generation shifting the NLL location while distributional shape remains stable.
A 7-feature ensemble achieves leak-free binary F1\,=\,0.694 under leave-one-generator-out evaluation, generalizing across model families.
The depth signal degrades substantially under instruction tuning, restricting current applicability to base models.
\end{abstract}

\section{Related Work}
\label{sec:related}

\subsection{AI-Generated Text Detection}
\label{sec:related-detection}

Methods for distinguishing human-written from machine-generated text have evolved from statistical tests \cite{gltr,grover,release_strategies} to zero-shot reference-model approaches \cite{detectgpt,fast_detectgpt,binoculars,dna_gpt} and learned classifiers that combine handcrafted features with neural architectures \cite{ghostbuster,feat_aug_transformer,abburi_multifaceted,reliable_detection,ld_score}.
Recent work pursues diverse signals including intrinsic dimensionality \cite{intrinsic_dimension}, surprisal diversity \cite{diveye}, and distributional gap measures \cite{generator_barrier}; see \citet{tang2024science}, \citet{wu_survey_2025}, and \citet{jawahar_survey} for surveys.
A persistent limitation is that these methods produce binary (real vs.\ synthetic) decisions.
Recent work moves beyond binary detection along several axes.
\citet{beyond_binary} classify text into four roles (human-only, LLM-polished, LLM-expanded, LLM-only) via involvement measurement, discriminating production \emph{modes} rather than recursive depth.
\citet{two_birds} jointly detect machine-generated text and attribute it to specific LLMs, and \citet{beyond_final_actor} distinguish dual creator-editor roles across four production modes.
Multi-generator attribution, including generator-level classification in SemEval 2024 Task 8 Subtask B \cite{semeval2024_task8} and the DeFactify dataset \cite{defactify_dataset}, discriminates among different \emph{sources}.
All these approaches classify text by its production process or authorship, while our depth classification tracks how many recursive generation steps a text has undergone, an orthogonal axis.
Even when detection scores correlate with depth, they exhibit high cross-generator variance as ordinal predictors (binary F1 from 0.52 to 0.71; Table~\ref{tab:baselines}), because each captures a single distributional property that generalizes inconsistently \cite{paraphrase_evades,detection_possibilities}.
Our contribution is not a new detection method but the task formulation (generation depth classification, framed within the ordinal classification literature \cite{gutierrez_ordinal_survey,coral_ordinal,corn_ordinal,frank_hall_ordinal}; ordinal approaches have been applied to sentiment analysis \cite{pang_opinion_mining} and essay scoring \cite{taghipour_neural_essay}) and the finding that combining drifting, intermediate, and near-stationary features yields consistent cross-generator performance.
This is orthogonal to source attribution \cite{uchendu_attribution,munir_looking_glass}, which identifies \emph{which} model generated text; our LOGO evaluation decouples generator identity from depth.

\subsection{Model Collapse and Iterative Generation}
\label{sec:related-collapse}

Iterative generation can degrade text quality through two distinct mechanisms: \emph{training-loop} drift, where models retrained on their own outputs progressively lose distributional coverage, and \emph{inference-chain} drift, where a fixed model generates text conditioned on its own prior output without retraining.
Self-consuming generative models progressively lose distributional coverage \cite{self_consuming_mad}, and model collapse is inevitable without fresh human data \cite{curse_of_recursion}, though careful data mixing can mitigate this \cite{model_collapse_avoidable,strong_model_collapse}.
Self-training and self-play approaches \cite{self_rewarding_lms,spin} also involve iterative self-generation but optimize a training objective; these studies focus on training-loop degradation, whereas our setting studies inference chains.
The distinction extends beyond setting: model collapse erodes distributional tail coverage irreversibly as training progresses \cite{curse_of_recursion,strong_model_collapse}. In contrast, the inference-chain drift we observe is fully reversible under fixed parameters, and distributional shape exhibits negligible depth effects (Cohen's $d < 0.10$; \S\ref{sec:results-differential}).
The drifting/intermediate/near-stationary tri-partition central to our analysis has no analogue in model collapse studies, which track aggregate divergence without separating location from shape components.
Two concurrent works are most directly relevant.
\citet{broken_telephone} analyze paraphrasing and translation chains, showing progressive information loss under semantic-preservation constraints that confine depth signal to surface-level lexical decay.
\citet{markovian_chains} demonstrate that such constraints induce Markovian attractor dynamics bounding distinguishable depth to approximately three classes.
Both study paraphrastic chains; we differ in three respects: (i) non-paraphrastic continuation chains permit richer drift (both semantic and distributional); (ii) handcrafted features enable the DDR decomposition into drifting, intermediate, and near-stationary components; and (iii) our tri-partition reveals \emph{what} converges (location) versus what remains stable (shape), while their analyses characterize \emph{that} convergence occurs.
That all three works independently converge on approximately three distinguishable classes reflects different mechanisms reaching the same ceiling: Markovian attractor dynamics in semantic space \cite{markovian_chains}, surface-level lexical decay under paraphrastic constraints \cite{broken_telephone}, and feature-space compression in continuation chains (inter-class KS drops from 0.28 to 0.09 after depth 2; this work).

\subsection{Vocabulary Diversity and Stylometry}
\label{sec:related-diversity}

Declining lexical diversity in LLM-generated text is documented in both training \cite{curious_decline} and deployment \cite{writing_diversity} settings.
Our surface features (TTR and hapax ratio) are classical stylometric measures \cite{stamatatos_survey,koppel_authorship,neal2017surveying}; more sophisticated alternatives exist (MTLD, HD-D \cite{mccarthy2010mtld}; MATTR \cite{covington2010mattr}) but TTR and hapax ratio suffice for depth discrimination.
We push beyond generator identity \cite{uchendu_attribution} to the \emph{depth} dimension under top-$p$ sampling \cite{nucleus_sampling}.

\subsection{Data Quality and Provenance}
\label{sec:related-provenance}

Scalable data curation relies on quality signals \cite{dsir,qurating,ccnet}, and recent work highlights the challenge of detecting training data contamination \cite{oren2024proving,golchin2024time} and maintaining data provenance at scale \cite{longpre2024data}.
Generation depth is a complementary provenance signal characterizing \emph{how many steps removed} text is from a human source.
Proactive watermarking \cite{watermark_llm,synthid_text,aaronson_watermark} embeds identifiable patterns, but watermark strength decays across multi-step chains \cite{chainwash}, which motivates passive post-hoc methods like ours.
At the feature level, our NLL analysis connects to \citet{min_k_percent}, who use the probability tail for membership inference; we analyze the full NLL distribution for generation depth classification.

\section{Results}
\label{sec:results}

\subsection{Depth Classification Performance}
\label{sec:results-classification}

The 7-feature ensemble achieves 3-class LOGO F1\,=\,0.762 (95\% CI [0.758, 0.766]; $N$\,=\,37{,}058) across eight generators from five families (Table~\ref{tab:logo-results}).
Because gen-0 seeds are shared across generators (\S\ref{sec:generation}), gen-0 classification is near-perfect (per-class F1\,$\approx$\,0.94) and the 3-class metric is inflated by this overlap.
We therefore adopt leak-free binary F1 (gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+)\,=\,0.694, CI [0.688, 0.700], as the primary metric throughout; it excludes gen-0 entirely and is unaffected by seed sharing.
Per-generator binary F1 ranges from 0.633 (Mistral-7B) to 0.724 (Pythia-2.8B), with the primary difficulty being gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+ discrimination (Appendix~\ref{app:confusion}).

\paragraph{Cross-model generalization.}
Cross-model chains (randomly selected generator per step) yield binary F1\,=\,0.764 under 5-fold CV.\footnote{Cross-model chains use the original five-generator subset (Pythia, OLMo, Qwen); Llama and Mistral were added later for single-generator evaluation. Sample-level CV is used because each chain contains multiple generators, making generator-level held-out splits inapplicable.}
Leave-one-family-out (LOFO) evaluation yields binary F1\,=\,0.686, confirming cross-family transfer.
A scale effect emerges: Pythia generators achieve the highest binary F1 (0.718--0.724), while larger models show degradation (Mistral-7B: 0.633), partly reflecting same-family affinity with the Pythia-410M reference model (cross-reference spread $\leq$0.013; \S\ref{sec:results-differential}).
Preliminary cross-domain evaluation suggests the signal persists with variation, though a domain$\times$temperature interaction exists (Appendix~\ref{app:domain}).
An end-to-end QLoRA classifier achieves 3-class F1\,=\,0.905 ($+$11.6\,pp; Appendix~\ref{app:qlora}), confirming that richer representations capture additional depth signal beyond the 7-feature set.

\paragraph{Length confound control.}
Length-matched subsampling yields binary F1\,=\,0.724 (vs.\ 0.770 unmatched); a random-subsample control confirms the drop reflects deconfounding, not sample-size reduction (Appendix~\ref{app:length}).

\paragraph{Seed-sharing control.}
Seed-level demeaning (F1\,=\,0.701) and an independent-seed experiment with disjoint seed pools (F1\,=\,0.680; Appendix~\ref{app:seed-control}) both confirm the classifier captures generative degradation, not seed-specific content.

\subsection{Differential Depth Response}
\label{sec:results-differential}

The primary structure in the feature space is a binary partition between \emph{drifting} and \emph{non-drifting} features ($k{=}2$ clustering, silhouette\,=\,0.632; Appendix~\ref{app:ddr-validation}).
Domain-informed criteria further resolve a \emph{differential depth response} (DDR) with a 3/1/3 characterization: \emph{drifting} features (entropy mean, TTR, hapax ratio) shift monotonically with depth; entropy std occupies a sole \emph{intermediate} position (large level shift, low monotonicity); and \emph{near-stationary} features (entropy max, tail decay, entropy min) show negligible depth effects (Cohen's $d < 0.10$ vs.\ $d > 0.75$ for drifting features; CV shift $<$3\% vs.\ $>$15\%).
This partition is robust under heteroscedasticity-corrected metrics (below).

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{fig1_differential_response.pdf}
\caption{Differential depth response: Spearman correlations between individual features and generation depth. Drifting features (hapax ratio, TTR, entropy mean) show $|\rho| > 0.60$; entropy std ($|\rho|{=}0.16$, $d{=}0.55$) is the sole intermediate feature; near-stationary features (entropy max, tail decay, entropy min) show $d < 0.10$ for gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+ (entropy min's elevated pooled $|\rho|$ reflects the gen-0/gen-1 boundary; \S\ref{sec:results-differential}).}
\label{fig:feature-drift}
\end{figure}

Pooled class-balanced Spearman correlations with depth confirm the split (Figure~\ref{fig:feature-drift}):
drifting features show substantial monotonic trends (hapax ratio $\rho = -0.64$, TTR $\rho = -0.63$, entropy mean $\rho = -0.60$),
while shape features remain near-stationary (tail decay $|\rho| = 0.04$; per-depth distributions in Appendix~\ref{app:feature-distributions}).
The six-fold magnitude gap between drifting ($|\rho| > 0.60$) and near-stationary features ($|\rho| < 0.10$) defines the DDR partition, with entropy std ($|\rho| = 0.16$, $d{=}0.55$) as the sole intermediate member; the 3/1/3 partition is stable across $d$ thresholds in $[0.56, 0.75]$: the drifting boundary reflects the natural gap between hapax ratio ($d{=}0.76$) and entropy std ($d{=}0.55$), and lowering it below 0.56 would reclassify entropy std as drifting despite its non-monotonic behavior ($|\rho|{=}0.16$). Data-driven clustering confirms the primary drifting/non-drifting split as the strongest structure ($k{=}2$, silhouette\,=\,0.632); the 3/1/3 refinement incorporates domain-informed criteria (binary-task Cohen's $d$) for entropy min's boundary status (Appendix~\ref{app:ddr-validation}).

\paragraph{Distributional shift quantification.}
Two-sample KS tests confirm the split: drifting-feature statistics (0.516--0.537) are ${\sim}10\times$ larger than shape-feature statistics (0.043--0.052; all $p \approx 0$ after Bonferroni correction).
Cohen's $d$ \cite{cohen1988statistical} (pooled, class-balanced) converges with $\rho$: drifting features show large effects (entropy mean $d{=}1.17$, TTR $d{=}0.88$, hapax ratio $d{=}0.76$), while shape features are near zero (entropy max $d{=}0.08$, tail decay $d{=}0.08$); Levene tests reject strict equal-variance ($p < 10^{-10}$); we therefore supplement pooled $d$ with Glass's $\Delta$ and Cliff's $\delta$ (Appendix~\ref{app:ddr-validation}), which confirm the partition with a ${\geq}9.5\times$ drifting-to-near-stationary gap.
Shape-feature CV shift ($<$3\% vs.\ $>$15\% for drifting features) supports ``near-stationary'' as a practical characterization.
Five features fall cleanly into the drifting or near-stationary groups under both $\rho$ and $d$; the remaining two require qualification: entropy min's pooled $|\rho|$ (0.40) reflects change concentrated at the gen-0/gen-1 boundary, but for gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+ it is near-stationary ($d{=}0.03$), placing it in the near-stationary group; entropy std shows a substantial level shift ($d{=}0.55$) despite low monotonicity ($|\rho|{=}0.16$), making it the sole intermediate feature.
The location/shape decomposition rests on the convergence of $\rho$, Levene, CV shift, and $d$, not the omnibus KS statistic alone.
Per-generator TOST equivalence testing confirms the partition is not a pooling artifact: entropy min passes equivalence ($|d| < 0.20$) for all eight generators, entropy max for six of eight, and tail decay for four of eight; all drifting features exceed the bound uniformly (Appendix~\ref{app:tost}).
Tail decay is near-stationary at the aggregate level ($d{=}0.08$, CV shift $<$3\%) with generator-dependent variation: the four non-passing generators show $d{=}0.15$--$0.22$, still far below the drifting threshold ($d > 0.75$).
Holdout generator validation (two 4/4 splits with swapped extreme-value generators) confirms partition stability: under simple joint thresholds the holdout produces a 3/2/2 partition (entropy min classified as intermediate due to elevated pooled $|\rho|$), but five of seven features are unambiguously classified, and entropy min's boundary status ($d < 0.06$ across all splits) is consistently resolved by the binary-task criterion (Appendix~\ref{app:tost}).

\paragraph{Feature complementarity.}
The full 7-feature set (F1\,=\,0.773) outperforms surface-only (0.688) and reference-only (0.713; McNemar $p \approx 0$; Appendix~\ref{app:ablation-table}).
Permutation importance: hapax ratio (0.35), entropy mean (0.23), TTR (0.18).
PCA confirms that the three drifting features share a single latent dimension: a single principal component explains 92.3\% of their joint variance, with near-uniform loadings (0.56--0.59; Appendix~\ref{sec:appendix-feature-correlation}).
The DDR partition thus distinguishes which features track this drifting dimension from those that remain depth-invariant, rather than claiming three independent depth signals.
TTR and hapax ratio are strongly correlated ($r = 0.97$); their permutation importance difference (0.35 vs.\ 0.18) reflects feature masking in tree-based ensembles \cite{strobl_conditional_2008}.
All three are retained for marginal LOFO gains (Appendix~\ref{app:lofo}).

\paragraph{Cross-family reference models.}
Alternative references (OLMo-2-1B, Qwen3-0.6B) achieve comparable LOGO F1 (spread 0.013; Table~\ref{tab:cross-ref} in Appendix~\ref{app:cross-ref}), with consistently negative entropy drift; this confirms the depth features are robust to reference model choice, though it does not alone establish DDR as a fundamental property of recursive generation.

\paragraph{Temperature and prompt-type sensitivity.}
The depth signal is modulated by decoding parameters and prompt type (Appendices~\ref{app:sampling-sensitivity},~\ref{app:prompt-type}).
All four tested generators degrade at $t{=}0.9$ ($-9.3$ to $-26.0$\,pp binary F1); low-temperature improvement is model-family-dependent ($+7$--$9$\,pp for Pythia/OLMo at $t{=}0.5$, negligible for Qwen).
Continuation chains show the strongest drift (binary F1\,=\,0.781), with cross-prompt-type transfer confirming shared signal (LOPTO F1\,=\,0.753).


\subsection{Comparison with Detection Baselines}
\label{sec:results-baselines}

To contextualize depth discrimination ability rather than claim competitive advantage over detection-optimized methods, we repurpose four detection scores as ordinal depth predictors using the same XGBoost framework and LOGO splits (Table~\ref{tab:baselines}).

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\footnotesize
\begin{tabular}{lcccc}
\toprule
\textbf{Method} & \textbf{Feat.} & \textbf{3-cl F1} & \textbf{Bin F1} & \textbf{ms/text} \\
\midrule
4-det.\ + surface     & 6 & \textbf{0.795} & \textbf{0.708} & 22.8 \\
4-detector ens.\      & 4 & 0.785 & 0.700 & 22.8 \\
7-feature (ours)      & 7 & 0.774 & 0.705 & \textbf{9.7} \\
Avg-LogProb           & 1 & 0.707 & 0.673 & N/A \\
FastDetectGPT         & 1 & 0.660 & 0.569 & N/A \\
LD-Score              & 1 & 0.630 & 0.675 & N/A \\
Binoculars            & 1 & 0.411 & 0.539 & N/A \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Depth classification (8-gen LOGO, pooled evaluation; slightly higher than per-generator macro average in Table~\ref{tab:logo-results}). Identical XGBoost configuration. 7-feature: one 410M model (905\,MB); 4-det ensembles: two models, 1.4B params (2{,}868\,MB). Individual detection scores (N/A) share the reference-model forward pass; per-method timing is not separately profiled.}
\label{tab:baselines}
\end{table}

The 7-feature ensemble exceeds all individual baselines in 3-class F1 ($\Delta$\,=\,6.7--36.3\,pp).
Multi-detector ensembles achieve marginally higher binary F1 (0.708 vs.\ 0.705) at 2.4$\times$ inference cost; that detection scores achieve comparable depth discrimination suggests depth information is implicitly encoded in distributional divergence measures, while our DDR decomposition makes this structure explicit.

\section{Discussion}
\label{sec:discussion}

The DDR tri-partition (3 drifting / 1 intermediate / 3 near-stationary) is consistent with a location/shape decomposition: under fixed temperature $\tau$ and nucleus $p$, the softmax output distribution's shape (variance, tail behavior) is constrained by the decoding configuration, while iterative conditioning shifts the input distribution's location as text becomes increasingly predictable to the reference model.
This interpretation is post-hoc and empirical; formal analysis of softmax output distribution dynamics under recursive conditioning remains an open problem.
DDR is an empirical decomposition capturing this dichotomy, not a claimed universal law of recursive generation.
DDR as characterized here is a parameter-dependent phenomenon (modulated by temperature and prompt type), not an intrinsic property of recursive generation independent of decoding conditions.
Temperature and prompt-type ablations (\S\ref{sec:results-differential}) support this as a tendency rather than a guarantee: all four tested generators degrade at $t{=}0.9$ ($-9.3$ to $-26.0$\,pp), and the signal varies across prompt types.

Instruction tuning substantially weakens the signal across all three tested families (OLMo, Qwen, Llama; Appendix~\ref{app:instruct}).
Within-model 3-class F1 drops 3.7--19.9\,pp (OLMo: 0.575 vs.\ 0.754; Qwen: 0.732 vs.\ 0.769; Llama: 0.544 vs.\ 0.742), while binary F1 changes remain small ($\Delta \leq 3.2$\,pp), indicating that instruction tuning primarily disrupts the gen-0/gen-1 boundary.
Under cross-generator evaluation, the degradation is larger (OLMo-Instruct LOGO F1\,=\,0.338 vs.\ 0.763 base).
Entropy-mean $\rho$ reverses sign consistently ($+0.48$ for OLMo and Qwen, $+0.23$ for Llama; all base models ${\approx}{-}0.6$), and 6 of 7 features reverse direction for OLMo and Qwen, 3 of 7 for Llama, consistent with instruction tuning shifting the generation attractor rather than destroying the iterative dynamics.
This restricts current applicability to base models; at the document level, within-model gen-1 per-class F1\,=\,0.63 (average across three instruct families; Appendix~\ref{app:instruct}) suffices for corpus-level flagging but not automated filtering (Appendix~\ref{app:error-analysis}).
Cross-temperature transfer degrades substantially at $t{=}1.0$ (Appendix~\ref{app:cross-temp}).
DDR characterizes distributional structure under recursive generation; depth profiling identifies this structure rather than prescribing data-selection actions.
A preliminary downstream experiment ($n{=}3$ seeds; Appendix~\ref{app:downstream}) provides suggestive but statistically underpowered evidence that depth composition may not determine training utility at fixed sample count; this observation requires validation at larger scale before drawing conclusions.

The QLoRA end-to-end classifier (3-class F1\,=\,0.905; Appendix~\ref{app:qlora}) confirms that richer representations capture depth signal well beyond the 7-feature set; at binary F1\,=\,0.694, the handcrafted ensemble trades classification ceiling for interpretability, enabling the DDR decomposition that end-to-end classifiers cannot provide.
Three classes represent the practical ceiling (5-class F1 ${\approx}$0.50; Appendix~\ref{app:finer-depth}), with the gen-1/gen-2+ boundary as the bottleneck.
Simulated human editing (token-level perturbation) suggests graceful degradation of the depth signal (Appendix~\ref{app:human-edit}), though the gap between simulated perturbation and real-world post-processing remains untested.
DDR is distinct from model collapse \cite{curse_of_recursion,strong_model_collapse}: inference-chain drift is fully reversible under fixed parameters and leaves distributional shape near-stationary ($d < 0.10$; variance ratios 0.98--1.12).

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

When LLM outputs are fed back as inputs to subsequent generation, the resulting recursive chains form a dynamical system whose distributional properties evolve with each step.
Characterizing the structure of this evolution is fundamental to understanding how base language models transform distributions under iterative conditioning, with relevance to understanding model collapse dynamics \cite{curse_of_recursion, self_consuming_mad}.
Yet binary detection decisions \cite{fast_detectgpt,binoculars,ld_score,detectgpt} obscure this structure: a first-generation continuation retains much of the source distribution's lexical properties, while deeper recursive text exhibits measurably reduced vocabulary diversity and compressed perplexity.

We formulate \emph{generation depth classification}, classifying text by generation depth (gen-0\,/\,gen-1\,/\,gen-2+) rather than a binary label, and term this \emph{depth profiling}.
No existing method provides a feature-level decomposition of depth signal in non-paraphrastic continuation chains.

The key finding is a \emph{differential depth response} (DDR) with a three-way partition: when we measure how eight base-model generators from five families (Pythia, OLMo, Qwen, Llama, Mistral; 0.6B--8B parameters) transform text across recursive depths, three \emph{drifting} features (reference-model mean entropy, type-token ratio, hapax ratio) shift monotonically (Cohen's $d > 0.75$), one \emph{intermediate} feature (entropy std) shows a non-monotonic level shift ($d{=}0.55$), and three \emph{near-stationary} features (entropy max, tail decay, entropy min) exhibit negligible depth effects ($d < 0.10$).
This is consistent with recursive generation shifting the NLL location while distributional shape remains stable under fixed sampling parameters.
While distributional drift under recursive generation is documented in the model collapse literature \cite{curse_of_recursion, self_consuming_mad}, the structured tri-partition and its exploitation for depth classification have not been previously reported.
We restrict to base (pretrained) models, since instruction-tuning introduces confounds that obscure this intrinsic mechanism (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).

A 7-feature ensemble combining all three groups achieves leak-free binary F1\,=\,0.694 under eight-generator leave-one-generator-out (LOGO) evaluation and 0.764 on cross-model chains, using a single 410M-parameter reference model (\S\ref{sec:results-baselines}).

Our contributions are empirical rather than methodological:
\begin{enumerate}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
    \item We formulate generation depth classification, moving beyond binary real-vs-synthetic detection to classify text as gen-0\,/\,gen-1\,/\,gen-2+, and construct an evaluation suite of 37{,}058 texts from eight base-model generators spanning five families (0.6B--8B parameters).
    \item We identify a \emph{differential depth response} (DDR) in base models: data-driven analysis reveals a primary drifting/non-drifting partition ($k{=}2$, silhouette\,=\,0.632); domain-informed criteria further resolve a 3/1/3 characterization (three drifting features, $|\rho| > 0.60$, $d{=}0.76$--$1.17$; one intermediate, $d{=}0.55$; three near-stationary, $d < 0.10$) with a ${\geq}9.5\times$ effect-size gap confirmed under heteroscedasticity-robust metrics (Appendix~\ref{app:ddr-validation}).
    \item We establish DDR's parameter dependence: instruction tuning reverses feature drift direction across three families (entropy mean $\rho$: $-0.60 \rightarrow +0.48$), and depth signal degrades at $t{=}0.9$ ($-9.3$ to $-26.0$\,pp) while remaining robust within $t \in [0.5, 0.7]$ (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).
\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{Data-Driven Clustering}

To assess whether the 3/1/3 DDR partition emerges from the data rather than post-hoc grouping, we apply $k$-means clustering ($k \in \{2,3,4,5\}$) to the seven features in standardized $(|\rho|, d)$ space (Table~\ref{tab:clustering}).

$k$ & Silhouette & Clusters \\

The primary drifting/non-drifting split ($k{=}2$, silhouette\,=\,0.632) is the strongest cluster structure.
At $k{=}3$, entropy min forms its own cluster rather than joining the near-stationary group because its pooled $|\rho|{=}0.40$ (driven by the gen-0/gen-1 boundary) places it far from other near-stationary features in $\rho$ space.
The 3/1/3 DDR partition resolves this by using the gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+ Cohen's $d$ ($d{=}0.03$) to place entropy min in the near-stationary group, a domain-informed refinement that unsupervised clustering cannot recover from pooled statistics alone.
At $k{=}4$ (silhouette\,=\,0.571), entropy std separates from the near-stationary group, consistent with its intermediate DDR classification.

\subsection*{TOST Equivalence Bound Sensitivity}
\label{app:tost-sensitivity}

Table~\ref{tab:tost-sensitivity} shows the fraction of generators for which each feature passes the TOST equivalence test (gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+, $\alpha{=}0.05$) at three equivalence bounds $\varepsilon$.

\subsection*{Holdout Generator Split Validation}
\label{app:holdout-split}

To confirm the DDR partition is not an artifact of the specific generator pool, we split the eight generators into disjoint selection (4) and validation (4) sets, compute per-subset pooled $(|\rho|, d)$, and check whether all seven features receive the same zone assignment in both subsets.
We evaluate two complementary splits to avoid dependence on a single partition:
Split~A selects \{Pythia-2.8B, Qwen3-1.7B, OLMo, Mistral\} (validation: Pythia-1B, Qwen3-0.6B, Qwen3-8B, Llama);

\subsection{Differential Depth Response}
\label{sec:results-differential}

The primary structure in the feature space is a binary partition between \emph{drifting} and \emph{non-drifting} features ($k{=}2$ clustering, silhouette\,=\,0.632; Appendix~\ref{app:ddr-validation}).
Domain-informed criteria further resolve a \emph{differential depth response} (DDR) with a 3/1/3 characterization: \emph{drifting} features (entropy mean, TTR, hapax ratio) shift monotonically with depth; entropy std occupies a sole \emph{intermediate} position (large level shift, low monotonicity); and \emph{near-stationary} features (entropy max, tail decay, entropy min) show negligible depth effects (Cohen's $d < 0.10$ vs.\ $d > 0.75$ for drifting features; CV shift $<$3\% vs.\ $>$15\%).
This partition is robust under heteroscedasticity-corrected metrics (below).

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{fig1_differential_response.pdf}
\caption{Differential depth response: Spearman correlations between individual features and generation depth. Drifting features (hapax ratio, TTR, entropy mean) show $|\rho| > 0.60$; entropy std ($|\rho|{=}0.16$, $d{=}0.55$) is the sole intermediate feature; near-stationary features (entropy max, tail decay, entropy min) show $d < 0.10$ for gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+ (entropy min's elevated pooled $|\rho|$ reflects the gen-0/gen-1 boundary; \S\ref{sec:results-differential}).}
\label{fig:feature-drift}
\end{figure}

Pooled class-balanced Spearman correlations with depth confirm the split (Figure~\ref{fig:feature-drift}):
drifting features show substantial monotonic trends (hapax ratio $\rho = -0.64$, TTR $\rho = -0.63$, entropy mean $\rho = -0.60$),
while shape features remain near-stationary (tail decay $|\rho| = 0.04$; per-depth distributions in Appendix~\ref{app:feature-distributions}).
The six-fold magnitude gap between drifting ($|\rho| > 0.60$) and near-stationary features ($|\rho| < 0.10$) defines the DDR partition, with entropy std ($|\rho| = 0.16$, $d{=}0.55$) as the sole intermediate member; the 3/1/3 partition is stable across $d$ thresholds in $[0.56, 0.75]$: the drifting boundary reflects the natural gap between hapax ratio ($d{=}0.76$) and entropy std ($d{=}0.55$), and lowering it below 0.56 would reclassify entropy std as drifting despite its non-monotonic behavior ($|\rho|{=}0.16$). Data-driven clustering confirms the primary drifting/non-drifting split as the strongest structure ($k{=}2$, silhouette\,=\,0.632); the 3/1/3 refinement incorporates domain-informed criteria (binary-task Cohen's $d$) for entropy min's boundary status (Appendix~\ref{app:ddr-validation}).

\paragraph{Distributional shift quantification.}
Two-sample KS tests confirm the split: drifting-feature statistics (0.516--0.537) are ${\sim}10\times$ larger than shape-feature statistics (0.043--0.052; all $p \approx 0$ after Bonferroni correction).
Cohen's $d$ \cite{cohen1988statistical} (pooled, class-balanced) converges with $\rho$: drifting features show large effects (entropy mean $d{=}1.17$, TTR $d{=}0.88$, hapax ratio $d{=}0.76$), while shape features are near zero (entropy max $d{=}0.08$, tail decay $d{=}0.08$); Levene tests reject strict equal-variance ($p < 10^{-10}$); we therefore supplement pooled $d$ with Glass's $\Delta$ and Cliff's $\delta$ (Appendix~\ref{app:ddr-validation}), which confirm the partition with a ${\geq}9.5\times$ drifting-to-near-stationary gap.
Shape-feature CV shift ($<$3\% vs.\ $>$15\% for drifting features) supports ``near-stationary'' as a practical characterization.
Five features fall cleanly into the drifting or near-stationary groups under both $\rho$ and $d$; the remaining two require qualification: entropy min's pooled $|\rho|$ (0.40) reflects change concentrated at the gen-0/gen-1 boundary, but for gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+ it is near-stationary ($d{=}0.03$), placing it in the near-stationary group; entropy std shows a substantial level shift ($d{=}0.55$) despite low monotonicity ($|\rho|{=}0.16$), making it the sole intermediate feature.
The location/shape decomposition rests on the convergence of $\rho$, Levene, CV shift, and $d$, not the omnibus KS statistic alone.
Per-generator TOST equivalence testing confirms the partition is not a pooling artifact: entropy min passes equivalence ($|d| < 0.20$) for all eight generators, entropy max for six of eight, and tail decay for four of eight; all drifting features exceed the bound uniformly (Appendix~\ref{app:tost}).
Tail decay is near-stationary at the aggregate level ($d{=}0.08$, CV shift $<$3\%) with generator-dependent variation: the four non-passing generators show $d{=}0.15$--$0.22$, still far below the drifting threshold ($d > 0.75$).

The full 7-feature set (F1\,=\,0.773) outperforms surface-only (0.688) and reference-only (0.713; McNemar $p \approx 0$; Appendix~\ref{app:ablation-table}).
Permutation importance: hapax ratio (0.35), entropy mean (0.23), TTR (0.18).
PCA confirms that the three drifting features share a single latent dimension: a single principal component explains 92.3\% of their joint variance, with near-uniform loadings (0.56--0.59; Appendix~\ref{sec:appendix-feature-correlation}).
The DDR partition thus distinguishes which features track this drifting dimension from those that remain depth-invariant, rather than claiming three independent depth signals.
TTR and hapax ratio are strongly correlated ($r = 0.97$); their permutation importance difference (0.35 vs.\ 0.18) reflects feature masking in tree-based ensembles \cite{strobl_conditional_2008}.
All three are retained for marginal LOFO gains (Appendix~\ref{app:lofo}).

\paragraph{Cross-family reference models.}
Alternative references (OLMo-2-1B, Qwen3-0.6B) achieve comparable LOGO F1 (spread 0.013; Table~\ref{tab:cross-ref} in Appendix~\ref{app:cross-ref}), with consistently negative entropy drift; this confirms the depth features are robust to reference model choice, though it does not alone establish DDR as a fundamental property of recursive generation.

The depth signal is modulated by decoding parameters and prompt type (Appendices~\ref{app:sampling-sensitivity},~\ref{app:prompt-type}).
All four tested generators degrade at $t{=}0.9$ ($-9.3$ to $-26.0$\,pp binary F1); low-temperature improvement is model-family-dependent ($+7$--$9$\,pp for Pythia/OLMo at $t{=}0.5$, negligible for Qwen).
Continuation chains show the strongest drift (binary F1\,=\,0.781), with cross-prompt-type transfer confirming shared signal (LOPTO F1\,=\,0.753).

\label{sec:results-baselines}

To contextualize depth discrimination ability rather than claim competitive advantage over detection-optimized methods, we repurpose four detection scores as ordinal depth predictors using the same XGBoost framework and LOGO splits (Table~\ref{tab:baselines}).

4-detector ens.\      & 4 & 0.785 & 0.700 & 22.8 \\

\caption{Depth classification (8-gen LOGO, pooled evaluation; slightly higher than per-generator macro average in Table~\ref{tab:logo-results}).
